utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Anna Richterova and Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with co-counsel Milan Trbojevic, Marela Jevtovic and Barbara Baruch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you all. Yes, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have three very short things. The first is I was informed by Ms. Korner that she will -- she is in the Stakic case right now until 4.00 and she would like to ask Your Honours if we could discuss the motion for adjournment of trial either after 4.00 or better towards the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no problem with that unless Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Mr. Ackerman has no problems with that so we will communicate later on to Ms. Korner whether the debate will take place at 4.00 or after 4.00 or towards the end of the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The other thing is we haven't received any response with respect to Prnjavor Rule 92 bis witnesses and because we already started calling the Prnjavor witnesses we would appreciate to know whether we need to call more witnesses than scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll have a response as soon as I can, Your Honour. I'm doing the best I can. I'll have it -- certainly I'll have it by Monday. That's -- that may be the best I can do because there is a lot of reading to do there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that satisfy you, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, we would appreciate it sooner but we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it just occurred to me there may be a way I can do it sooner and if I can I'll certainly do it. I want to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could do it in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to do it as quickly as I can, Your Honour, please understand that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Like we've done in the past. I think we could live with that too and it would facilitate the burden of the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The last thing relates to the photographs, Mr. Odobasic's photographs in question. And I was told it would be advisable to discuss this not in his presence. I just want to inform the Court that I spoke to the investigator who took the statement in -- on 15th of March, 1999. He didn't have a clear recollection of taking the statement but because he put the words, "I am providing the investigator with these photos," he believed that he got the photos. Then I checked the so-called information index form, which is a form which always had to be -- have to be filled in after a piece of evidence is brought to the OTP, and I found out that really, on 15th of March, 1999, this investigator received the photos. It says that they are photos of injuries resulting from beatings in 1993. It was most probably the reason why we didn't pay too much attention to them, because it was outside of the period covered in our indictment. So there was absolutely nothing behind the fact that we didn't disclose them. We weren't hiding any evidence. And me personally, I saw these pictures on Sunday during the proofing, and I returned these photos to the witness, informing him that I do not intend to use them as evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope I didn't indicate in any way that I had a concern about the Prosecutor's failure to disclose. Because they were outside the indictment but my concern, I think that I expressed, was that the witness told us under oath that he had never given these to the Prosecutor and that concerns me and that's what I asked that we look into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I intend to take it up with the witness after you finished with your cross-examination, in fact, Mr. Ackerman. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman? Yes, but we haven't got the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll just be here in case he comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Odobasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I hope we will be able to terminate, to finish your testimony today but before you continue, may I ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you rest well and are you ready for another day in court?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When we broke yesterday we were talking about your departure from Prnjavor and I had asked you if you were actually expelled from Prnjavor and that's when you told us that you had some photographs you'd like us to look at. And that's where I want to take up today. The person who signed that authorisation, who you gave the authorisation to, the lawyer Branislav Malic, he's a friend of yours, is he not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to those photographs you showed us yesterday, I want you to understand that I think all of us who saw them were shocked by them and we believe that no human being should be allowed to do that to any other human being and I want to express at least the sympathy of the Defence to you for what happened to you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very noble from you, and I should like to express my gratitude to you for that. I wouldn't wish any of that to happen to any human being in this world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I would hope that whoever is responsible for that, if they have not yet been punished, will be.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anyone was ever punished. These individuals are still working in the town of Prnjavor. They haven't had to face any consequences whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us their names. I think the world should know their names. Who are they? They are a couple of reserve police officers, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten up on two occasions in the police station and on the basis of that, I concluded they were not members of the reserve force. I was beaten up two times in the premises of regular police and two times in my own home. The individuals in question were the following, Vlado Budak, Pero Jankovic, Darko Savic, Milan Jelic, a man by the surname of Pancic, a certain Sestic Pokrac [phoen]. I was beaten by six police officers and I was taken to the police station pursuant to an order of a then inspector of the police station, Milan Jelic, who had sent two policemen to fetch me on one of these occasions when I was beaten up. They took me to the police station and on the other occasion I was taken at 3.00 a.m. to the police station and again was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you and I think other members of your family were beaten at your home by two policemen, you called Mr. Malic to come to your house following that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not two policemen. I said six policemen, sir. And Mr. Malic is a friend of mine, was one of the very few Serbs who dared to come to see me two days later and it was on that occasion that we talked about this power of attorney that I had to give to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You asked him to assist you in your efforts to get away from Prnjavor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't take part in my departure. I only asked him to take this power of attorney so that he could take care of my property, my father's property and my brother's property, and three such powers of attorney were made for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I need to have the Prosecutor give you back your statement of 30 January, 1999, please. If you look at the very last page, it's the third paragraph up from the bottom. What you told the Prosecutor at that time was that you had actually tried to leave Prnjavor on two occasions before you finally succeeded in doing so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had the documents prepared allowing you to go to Sarajevo but both times you tried to leave you were taken off the bus and they would not let you leave; true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a mistake. I did not have documents to go to Sarajevo. I only had documents allowing me to go to the west, to Serbia, Hungary and further on to Sweden. It was my wish to go to Sarajevo, Mr. Ackerman, after Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So where the statement says, "I had already had documents prepared in Ljubljana so I could go to Sarajevo," that you tell us was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not a mistake. I obtained documents from Prnjavor authorities and I needed to have a visa for Sweden so we had to buy visas or sometimes we got them from Sweden, and through a set of circumstances, a Serb from Sarajevo visited me at my house and he offered that we swap three of our houses for his house in Sarajevo, and we made a contract to that effect with him, and my plan was that a part of the family should go further on to Sweden and that I should go to Sarajevo to check on the condition of that house before taking it over, because we didn't have accommodation in Sarajevo and I wanted to check what the condition of the house was so that my family could eventually be accommodated there. As for the documents, we are talking here about passports, in Ljubljana, we had the closest embassy that we could get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, please slow down as much as you can because the interpreters really have to work hard to catch up with you with the speed with which you're talking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you remember about when these two times were that you had tried to leave and were taken off the bus and were not permitted to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 3rd of June until the 27th of July, when I left. During that period of time, we were always ready to leave, and on the eve of our departure, the night before, Braco Milijasevic would come to our house. He was some sort of leader at the Prnjavor police station, whether he was a deputy commander, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going to be here tomorrow if you cannot just listen to my question and answer it. The only question I really wanted to have you answer was about when were the two times that you tried to leave and were not permitted to. That's all I want to know. I don't need the other answers. Can you just tell us that? I think you said between 3 June and 27 July, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he said, Mr. Ackerman, and I think that should suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that your position, that it was sometime between those dates but you don't know precisely?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just that one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my position. It happened during that period of time. And full allow me just one more sentence, the gentleman in question came to my house on two occasions and he said, "Gentlemen, you are not able to leave. You will not be able to leave tomorrow." And I think that he once added one more sentence. He said something to the effect, "Until your wounds are healed."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you weren't actually on the bus and taken off the bus, you were taken off the list of people who were allowed to get on the bus? Is that a more accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't allow us to go. He said that my family could not leave the town in any manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I really do understand that. And what I'm trying to clear up, your statement on page 11 was that you had tried twice to leave town, to go to Hungary. "Both times they took me off the bus and wouldn't let me leave." Now, I concluded from that that you were on the bus and they had taken you off the bus before it left. Am I wrong in making that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right about the bus. It is true that we were ready, we had our bags packed and we were ready to leave, and on two occasions we were not allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: Were you on the bus --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you actually on the bus and then taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, because I was not allowed to get to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then after you say both times they took me off the bus and wouldn't let me leave, you then say this: "The rest of my family also voluntarily got off the bus." Now, do you understand that I could have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mistaken that to mean that you and your family were on a bus and you were taken off and they voluntarily got off of that bus?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're right. You made your conclusion on the basis of what it says here but I think that this was not properly formulated. Getting to the bus meant going away into the freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm satisfied with your answer, sir. I want to talk to you now about your property in Prnjavor. Prosecution Exhibit P1766, that's the authorisation that you gave to Branislav Malic, lists property as a plot of land cadastre number 373/3, arable land called Kuciste housing 551 square metres, registered in the land registry as street number 214, Prnjavor, and an office building located on that property. Now, I know that in your mind you have a picture now of that property that's described in that authorisation and what I want to ask you is: Is that the same property that was later known as the property at Avdo Tesnjak number 1 or is it a different property?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo Tesnjak is the name of a street, and before the war, the name was later changed. This is reference to the property located in the Avdo Tesnjak Street which later changed its name into Milos Todic or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a different piece of property than that contained in this authorisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any other property except for this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this authorisation refers to property that's called Kuciste and it's at street number 214, and you're telling us that's the same property that was located at Avdo Tesnjak number 1? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You remained in possession of this property until February of 1994, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in my possession. It remained in my possession in the land survey records but practically speaking, it was confiscated on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you -- it was confiscated in February of 1994 and not before that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was confiscated in February of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then this property was later returned to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not returned, but the UN human rights chamber in Sarajevo ordered that the property should be returned, and I think it was returned in the year of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in addition, Republika Srpska was ordered to pay you 20.720 convertible marks as pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for the illegal taking of your property; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was the money ever paid?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a year and a half, it was not paid, and pursuant to an order of the OHR, it was finally paid in November last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The order of the Court ordered that you also receive 10 per cent interest for any unpaid portion of that amount. So did they also pay you the 10 per cent interest during that period of time when they hadn't paid it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within one month, they paid out both the principal and the interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you I want to go through this just as briefly as I can, a couple of questions about your work with the -- I think the commission for missing persons, that's the name of it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State commission for tracing the missing persons, and the federal commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was also a Republika Srpska commission for missing persons in operation too; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, and it exists to this day. There used to be a commission of the HVO also in the past but it ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And have you on occasion been involved in excavations that were being conducted by the Republika Srpska commission for missing persons? Exhumations involving Muslims or -- excavations involving Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is unclear. Could you please clarify? These are two different notions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll try to make it clearer. Let me just ask you this: Have you ever been in a location where an excavation was being carried out when IFOR was present and when the Republika Srpska Commission for Missing Persons was present?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any exhumation taking place in the other entity is always attended by both commissions as well as representatives of IPTF and other international institutions. So far I have attended a number of exhumations both taking place in one entity and in the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's exactly what I was looking for. Have you always proceeded correctly in the -- in these matters regardless when of whether the exhumations were of Serbs or Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to explain what do you mean when you say proceeded correctly? Or shall I explain it to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll go directly to the point. Do you recall being involved in an exhumation that was taking place in 1977 at I think a couple of locations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, 1997, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At Stog and at Mount Poljenik?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was at the time that you mentioned but I was present with the commission of Republika Srpska at Stog, Poljenik, and some other locations. Naturally, you should be aware of duties and tasks of each commission during such exhumations in order to understand the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a moment? I should have given documents to the Prosecutor and yourselves before I started and could I get that done before I go any further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I don't intend to use these as exhibits but I've distributed them just for the purpose of demonstrating a good faith basis for the questions that I'll ask next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to read you a portion of a report starting -- it's starting on page 5 of a document from the Slobodna Bosna of September the 13th, 2001. I'm just going to read this to you, sir, and simply ask you if it is true or not and that's all I'm really interested in with regard to it. The report reads, "At the Mount Poljenik location, 12 corpses of former soldiers of the Srbac Brigade were discovered. During the forensic examination, IFOR informed the Serbian team that all approaches to the location have been blocked by women from Srebrenica who live in the area. They were really women from Srebrenica and it was obvious that Jasmin Odobasic, the deputy of Amor Masovic incited them to do that, one of the eye witnesses of this event said." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page are you reading from, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the bottom of page 5, Your Honour, very bottom of page 5 and carrying over on to page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is true, Mr. Ackerman? Because you've got more than one statement in the part that you read. Are you referring to the last part or to the previous part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it true that he incited these women from Srebrenica to block access to those bodies that had been discovered?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a blatant lie. They heard that there had been some problems there but I was not present at the location at all, nor did I talk anybody into doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I need to read you the next part and simply ask you if this part is true. "At the recommendation of IFOR, the commission withdrew, leaving its equipment and the exhumed corpses. When they came back after a few days, the exhumed bodies were found collected on a pile and incinerated and one corpse was left on a stretcher. We found it very odd that one body was placed separately like that so we walked up to it very carefully. As it turned out the stretcher was mined and connected to an antitank mine with some explosives. Odobasic, who continuously observed the work of the Serbian forensic team commented the site of the complicated explosives mechanisms by saying the women were Srebrenica prepared that for you." Were you there and did you say that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is yet another blatant lie. I was present there and I was the one who escorted and provided security for the commission of Republika Srpska on the second occasion and this confirms that on the first occasion they came without announcement, without observing the procedures and rules. Now, Mr. Ackerman, had somebody known that there was a mine there, would they have approached the area and exposed themselves to the risk? They would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's a risky business to rely upon things that are printed in newspapers? One probably should not do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, Mr. Odobasic. Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to your statement now, sir, of 30 January, 1999. You talked on -- it's page 8 of the English version, there is a paragraph that begins with, "In that period," and I think you're talking about basically the summer of 1992. The paragraph deals with the shooting of some civilians. There was an Asim Kvasic, a car mechanic, who you think was named Nazir, and that person you think was killed by Gojko Kusic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who was Gojko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the members of the paramilitary formation, Wolves from Vucjak. He was also from the village of Kremna, which is very close to the place where their commander resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You said that Mile Beus was killed because the Serbs wanted money from him. Do you know who killed him?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How do you know that he was killed because the Serbs wanted money from him?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic told me that he had talked to the family of Mr. Beus and that the family had told him that money was sought from Mr. Beus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So did the family see the people who killed him?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. You have to ask them that. Perhaps the people who did it wore masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What -- I assume that it's your -- what you're telling us is that whoever those Serbs were that killed him were the Serbs that wanted money from him. It wasn't that all the Serbs in Prnjavor were after his money, was it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't even entertain such ideas, sir. There are many wonderful, noble, honest Serbs everywhere, including Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't have any idea then who it was who killed this person, who, what organisation they might have represented, whether they were under orders to do that or any such thing, do you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As far as you know, it was a bunch of criminals conducting a robbery-murder?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your assessment, sir. I don't know who might be behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked both in your statements and in your testimony about persons being dismissed from their positions, and when I say dismissed from their positions I'm talking about their positions within various enterprises in Prnjavor. First of all, do you know what it is I'm getting ready to ask you about?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about the persons dismissed, if we are talking about the same issue, then, yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Same issue. Who is it that you contend ordered these dismissals?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that the authorities ordered for them to be dismissed. This is supported by the fact that one of the main representatives of those authorities toured various enterprises, insisting on dismissals. People who were dismissed were in all walks of life. Those who sweep streets and those who held highest offices in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say the authorities, you mean those people who had gotten posts of authority as a result of the victory of the SDS in the multi-party elections? That's who you mean when you say authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the order came from political authorities, and it was implemented by those who held leading positions in enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And had the war broken out yet before these dismissals occurred? It had, hadn't it? That war was actually going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The persons who were dismissed were all persons who were not - I think we discussed this a little bit yesterday - not sympathetic with the concept of Republika Srpska, and therefore, not permitted to continue to oversee these socially owned enterprises; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, no. The largest number of those people were apolitical. They had nothing to do with politics. Nor did they assess whether they liked Republika Srpska or not. They were ordinary people who in most cases did not want to go and take part in the war, that they didn't consider their own. Those were ordinary people who were in somebody's way because they had apartments in downtown area. Then those were people who held offices which were very important for implementing the SDS policies, people who had an insight into the weaponry that was stored and existed in Prnjavor in various locations, and several other similar positions which they considered important, even ordinary shoe makers who worked in the factory had been dismissed and they had nothing to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will come to that. You told us yesterday that back before the multi-party elections, before the multi-party system, that you yourself were also apolitical, that you were not involved in politics, but you were told that to keep a position that you had, it was necessary that you be a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. member of the League of Communists. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That pertained to the period when I was head of the city inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Doesn't make much difference to me when it had to do with. It had to do with an apolitical person being told that they must be a member of a certain party to maintain their position. That's the case, isn't it? That's what happened with you. An ordinary, apolitical person was told they had to be a member of a certain party to maintain their position. Not that they had to be political, that they just had to be a member the party. Right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the only party was the League of Communists, in the period of time that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. The question I asked you was simple. You were told that you had to be a member of the communist party, League of Communists. You didn't have to be an active member. You didn't have to go out and do all kinds of communist things, but you did have to be a member of the party, didn't you? That's an easy question to answer. You can either answer it yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that's how it was during that period of time, when I held the office that I described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly that period of time that I was asking you about, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you a bit about the economy of Prnjavor. It's the case, isn't it, that most factories stopped production completely or only worked at 10 to 20 per cent of their pre-war capacity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Beginning in 1992, Your Honour. And progressively thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to go into numbers when we are speaking about the production, but any war will leave an impact on the manufacturing process. I don't know how it compared to the pre-war period of time because information of that nature is not accessible to me. I heard that the majority of those factories continued working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to now be able to look at your statement of 30 September, 1994, given to the security services centre of the state security services sector in Sarajevo. Do you remember giving a statement to them, sir?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is a statement that you gave just almost immediately after having gotten out of Prnjavor. Same year that you left Prnjavor; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 5 in the English version. It's a paragraph beginning with the language, "Characteristics of the Prnjavor economy." It reads, "Characteristics of the Prnjavor economy can be seen from the fact that most of the factories either stopped production completely or worked at 10 to 20 per cent of their pre-war capacity." Now, that's what you said in 1994, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at the last page of that document and tell me if your signature appears there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing you said was this: That as of 30 September, 1994, when you made this statement at least, Sloga footwear, that you worked for, went from 1.370 down to 200 employees; correct? It's the next sentence after the one I just read to you from that statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Standard furniture, formerly employed 200, now completely stopped. Your words were halted production completely. Same page, sir, just a little further down.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Same page you were just looking at, just below the information about Sloga footwear, right under the name Milorad Kovacevic. It's the next sentence after the one saying Milorad Kovacevic. It says the "standard furniture factory," find it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going to stay on this same page, it's the next sentence, pioneer clothing formerly 300 workers, now closed. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Metalka chain factory, formerly 260, reduced to 130. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was able to keep its 130 employees because it was marketing its products in Russia and Serbia and therefore at least had part of its pre-war market intact. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Jelsingrad crane factory, formerly 180 employees, now closed.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Gradip GIK, a building construction industrial combine. Used to employ 350 workers, not working now. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How close did the war, the actual fighting, that was going on in the war, how close did that get to Prnjavor, during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You pick a year. I want the year that it got closest to Prnjavor while you were there, how close did the fighting get to Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the closest combat went on in Derventa which is 30 some kilometres and when the Serbian army took Derventa and Brod, those were the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on the closest front line was in Bihac area, some 150 to 200 kilometres and on the other side, around Tesanj which is over 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. This same statement now, I'm now going to page 8, there is an extremely long paragraph, General Momir Talic's name is contained in the second line of that paragraph, which may be something that will help you find it. And quite a ways down in that paragraph, you say, "So far," and I assume that means up until around September of 1994, when you made this statement, you say, "So far, more than 300 Chetniks have been killed in clashes with soldiers of the BH Army on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality. And the number of wounded exceeds this figure several times over." Those are your words, aren't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would speak of fighting much closer than Derventa wouldn't it? You say it took place on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, there was never any fighting in the territory of the Prnjavor municipality. Deep into the territory of the municipality of Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say that they were killed in clashes with soldiers of the BH Army on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality, is that not true? Did you sign a statement that was not true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wording is not accurate. In the Prijedor [As interpreted] municipality, there was never any fighting. Except for the fighting that -- no, I mean there was no fighting whatsoever in that area. You cannot call fighting an attack on the village of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, saying the wording is not accurate is another way of saying that it's not true, and what you're saying is what this statement says that you signed is not true. So you signed an untrue statement. Isn't that a fair conclusion for me to make?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Here it is considered that about 30 members of the VRS from the Prnjavor municipality were killed, and I'm sure that this is what I stated as to what -- as to your interpretation, that's different. One can interpret this in the territory of the Prnjavor municipality, both in terms of territory and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour page 23, line 13 says Prijedor when it should say Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose you're correct, Mr. Ackerman, so that goes down for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you found the part of your statement that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see the part that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It starts with, "So far," and it says -- it ends with "the number of wounded exceeds this figure several times over." What I'd like you to do is read that sentence and I'd like the interpreters to interpret from what he reads rather than the document so we can see if the interpretation here is correct. So would you just read it in your language and we will have the interpreters tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the current fighting with the members of the BH Army, in the territory of Prijedor [As interpreted] municipality, more than -- in the territory of the Prnjavor municipality, more than 300 Chetniks were killed, whereas the number --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Read it again more slowly, sir, they are having trouble keeping up with you. Try to read it slowly because this is hard for them.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the fighting so far with the members of the BH army, in the Prnjavor municipality, more than 300 Chetniks were killed, whereas the number of wounded exceeds several times this figure."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the translation is correct. What you said was 300 Chetniks were killed in fighting in the Prnjavor municipality and the number of wounded exceeded that by several times. That's what you said in 1994, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. When I say 300 Chetniks in the Prnjavor municipality, I'm referring to the people from the municipality of Prnjavor, and it is implied that since there was no fighting in the Prnjavor municipality, that I was referring to the people who were killed elsewhere but were by origin from the Prnjavor municipality. Everyone knew that there was no fighting in the Prnjavor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think we could all accept that if you didn't use the words that "this happened on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality." Those are your words. "On the territory of the Prnjavor municipality." Not 300 Chetniks from the Prnjavor municipality but on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality. Now, if you signed a statement that was not true, you can tell us that and that will clear this up. It could have been a mistake but it's clearly what this says you said.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sir, it is clear there was no fighting whatsoever in the territory of Prnjavor municipality. In this sentence, I was referring to the people who were residents of the Prnjavor municipality and who got killed. That was the meaning of the sentence that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop this. It is -- what is being put to you is a very simple matter, Mr. Odobasic. What you are explaining now is not reflected in what appears in your statement. So Mr. Ackerman is telling you first of all is observing that still even though this does not reflect what you had in mind of saying, to say, you still signed it as it is. And you are being asked to explain. This is all that it is about. He is not accusing you of deliberately lying or telling an untruth at any point in time in the course of this statement. So what is your explanation for the discrepancy that there is between what you signed for here and what you are explaining now? There must be an explanation. I mean usually it's a very simple explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The explanation is very simple. Me and other people at that time knew that there was no fighting in the Prijedor -- Prnjavor municipality and I was referring to the residents of the Prnjavor municipality who got killed elsewhere. I was not referring to any fighting in the Prnjavor municipality because there was no such fighting. Maybe the commas or not correct after this first part of my sentence when I say in the fighting with the members of the BH army or maybe it's a typo. I don't know. But at any rate, territorially speaking I was referring to the people who lived there who were residents of that area but who got killed elsewhere because there was no fighting in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you say that more than 300 Chetniks had been killed, would that be in addition to the number of Serbian soldiers who were killed?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm wondering if you make any distinction between Chetniks and regular Serbian soldiers or if there are additionally Serbian soldiers who were killed in the fighting and you're just referring to Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. When you say regular soldiers, what regular soldiers do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very simple question. Again I'm going to intervene because I'm getting fed up now. What do you mean by Chetniks? Do you include under that term all the Serb soldiers or just one category of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to all Serb soldiers, the total number is 300, those who got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About three pages further, sir, on page 11 of this statement, in the English version it's a paragraph that begins with the words, "After breaking through the famous corridor and capturing Derventa."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you say there is, "The number of Chetniks killed rapidly increased with the number of new fronts." Now, again, are you using that term to include all Serbian soldiers? Or just those who styled themselves Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the term that was used for Serb soldiers generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A derogatory term, wasn't it, in some ways?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending for whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 13 of that same statement, you speak of the destruction of a Muslim mausoleum at Turbe. You said it was destroyed by Vlado Vasic from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Gornja Mravica, who was between 35 and 40 years old; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll see if I can help you. It might be easy for you to find the name Gajanin, Mehinovic, Karadjordje cafe. It's just under those.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you need me to repeat the question now?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that sentence you talk about the destruction of a Turbe by Vlado Vasic, and a person between 35 and 40 years old; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know what ethnicity Vlado Vasic was?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How do you know that he was the one who destroyed this place?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who live in a nearby village told me this, a village close to this facility, and also by a person who lives in this village where this facility was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And soon after it happened, this Vlado Vasic was found with his throat slashed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told this by the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, apparently from what you said about how you came by the information, it was rather generally known around that village that Vlado Vasic had been the one that had done this destruction?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember attending a funeral in this village, and being told this immediately after the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea who it was that killed Vlado Vasic, slit his throat?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I have any idea on who it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I thought maybe you had heard later that someone had been found out for having done it but if you haven't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably the same local police that was in charge of the case. You should check with them, whether they have any information to that effect or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not saying the local police were the ones that slit his throat, are you, or probably the ones who did it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. I said that they were probably in charge of the investigation, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, page 24, line 16, you were asked by Ms. Richterova about the departure of people from Prnjavor, non-Serbs, your answer in part was, "As early as 1992, in the second half of it, the so-called organised departures from Prnjavor started," and I'd just like you to tell us, if you can remember, when it was that the first of these, as you say, so-called organised departures occurred from the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, of course, but I can easily find out because two of my cousins were beaten up and expelled in that year. They went by one of those buses to Sweden. One has remained in Sweden and one has returned to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you told us yesterday that it was in the second half of 1992. I assume that could be July or August or somewhere in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was much later, towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Would you agree that the largest number of departures from Prnjavor occurred in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement that you gave in Sarajevo, page 13, the one we were just looking at, you said this, and it's right under the -- just right under the one about the Turbe: "Throughout 1993, the pressure on the non-Serb population increased and in this period, the largest number of Muslims and Croats were expelled. I know that every Saturday in March, April, May and June, about a dozen buses left Banja Luka for Sweden carrying the largest number of Prnjavor inhabitants." Now, I read that to say that the largest number of non-Serbian departures from Prnjavor occurred in 1993, because that's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't give me -- give the time frame work. The largest number of people left in the last wave in 1995. As for the years that I was still in Prijedor, it was at that time that the most -- that most of the people were expelled, but it was in 1995 that the largest exodus of Croats and Muslims took place. Between the 27th or rather after the 27th of July, I don't know. After I left. I know that a lot of people were coming to Zenica but I don't know the exact number so as far as the period of time that I was referring to, this is correct. This is when the largest exodus occurred, and I learned about 1995 only once that I arrived in the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that people were not permitted to leave Prnjavor until they had done a number of things, including having paid their water bills and their power bills and their other debts. Do you think it's somehow was oppressive to make sure that people had paid their debts to keep them from leaving without having paid their debts? Was that oppressive in some way?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are imposing that on a four- or five-year-old child, then it's more than an oppressive measure. If you need to prove that the child is not a military-age man -- I mean it's common knowledge at what age people become liable for military service in any country in the world. If my 70-year-old father must have such a certificate, he who was released from that duty a long time ago, then it was really an oppressive measure. Well, that was an interesting answer. Now, let me repeat my question and see if you can answer it. You told us that people were not permitted to leave Prnjavor until they had done a number of things including having paid their water bills, their power bills and their other debts. Do you think it's oppressive to make sure that people had paid their debts to keep them from leaving without having paid their debts? Was that oppressive in some way? Now, answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is limited only to the requirement that before one left Prnjavor, one had to settle all outstanding bills related to electricity, water and so on. This is what it is -- the question is being limited to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's only logical. Bosniaks are famous in Bosnia-Herzegovina for fulfilling their obligations but it would have been normal to bring a certificate from your work organisation or just a copy of the last bill that you paid. That should have been enough for them to let you go, but most of these certificates, when the last one -- as far as the last one is concerned, it was the one that was issued from the Secretariat for National Defence and it was the most difficult certificate to obtain. The main one, however, was the one on abandoning of property, and it was only once you have collected all these certificates that you were given the certificate from the Secretariat for National Defence. Nobody ever tried to avoid any of these obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, at page 28, line 16, Ms. Richterova asked this question: "And I would like to ask you one more question about these departures. Can you just briefly tell us, if you know, what made these people leave? Leave the municipality of Prijedor." And your answer was this: "It was the pressure that these people were subjected to on a daily basis and it was it was economically non-viable for them to remain there. All of the people who had been dismissed from work lost their income, medical insurance, health insurance." Now we are talking about people who had lost jobs because, among other things, all of these factories, all of these enterprises in Prnjavor, either stopped working at all or dramatically reduced their workforce; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I said to leave the municipality of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please answer that question, Mr. Odobasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The economic situation was only one reason for these departures. There were many other reasons, such as unbearable pressure to leave. I can enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, again that's not the question I asked you, sir. It's an interesting answer. I must admit your answers are all interesting but it would be nice if they had something to do with my questions. The question I asked you was a very simple question: When you talked about people who lost their -- who were dismissed from work, and therefore, lost their income, medical insurance and health insurance, you're including people who no longer had work because all of these enterprises either stopped working completely or dramatically reduced their workforces, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you changed your question, Mr. Ackerman. Before you didn't say included. Before you said now we are talking about people who had lost their jobs. So which one --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll ask the latter one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The latter one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's probably more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I think so too. We are waiting for your answer and the question very simply put if I would rephrase it for you, is when you said -- when you referred to all these persons who left Prnjavor inter alia because they had been dismissed from their employment, and therefore, they had lost their income, medical insurance, were you referring only to those Muslims and other non-Serbs that had been dismissed from their employment because of their ethnic -- ethnicity? Because of their ethnicity? Or were you also including others who had lost their job because of the economic situation then prevailing in Prnjavor? In other words, were you grouping them all together or were you referring only to one of these two groups?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to a part of those people, because regardless of the fact that the capacities were decreased as far as the production is concerned, Serbs remained in most of the cases. They had retained their status. I was referring to the people who had been thrown out from these companies and whose employment had been terminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you're saying is that the end result of the economic crisis and the predicament that these companies or factories or whatever they are, business concerns, business enterprises, found themselves in, the ones who lost the jobs were the Muslims and not the Serbs? Or were the non-Serbs and not the Serbs? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about the people who had lost their jobs, I was referring to non-Serbs, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Ackerman? I think that should satisfy you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your position, then, I guess, that before the war, 90 per cent of the people employed in these enterprise that is we discussed were Muslims and Croats? And that those were the one who is lost their jobs and the 10 per cent who remained were all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Big mistake. It is not true that 90 per cent of them were Muslims and Croats. I was referring to the number of the employed, that is the 90 per cent of the workforce, of course the ethnic structure was such that there were many more Serbs that were employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, 90 per cent of the jobs were lost because of the closures of these factories, only 10 per cent of the jobs remained after all these closures; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You must clarify this because we can't stay lost in the clouds. I will put to you some questions myself. Do you -- is it your belief, is it your contention, that there were non-Serbs who lost their jobs because they were dismissed for no other reason but their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated clearly that the largest number of those who were dismissed were those who refused to respond to mobilisation. I said clearly yesterday that there was a minimal number of Serbs who had been dismissed for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were there others, both Muslim, both non-Serbs and Serbs who were dismissed from their employment, from their jobs, not because of their ethnicity or because they had failed to respond to the mobilisation call, but because of the economic rundown that there was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know such people. I can't answer that question because I don't know in each individual case who was dismissed because of what reason. What I stated was in general terms. It is logical that there were such who had been dismissed because of the economic situation, and this is perhaps why they had to leave the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last -- my last question is this: Amongst this latter category of individuals, those, in other words, who were dismissed because of the degenerating economic situation at the time, was it only the non-Serbs that found themselves having to leave, opting to leave, Prnjavor, or was it also the Serbs? Were these Serbs and the non-Serbs who lost their jobs for this reason only for the economic situation in the same position? Or would you say that they were in a different position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of non-Serbs was worse. The Serbs who left town much more frequently left it due to ideological rather than economic reasons. I have to tell you that before the war, that municipality had several thousand of its residents working abroad and many Serbs decided that it was better for them to go and live in other countries, and that was the most frequent reason for their departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's stop here for the time being, Mr. Ackerman. And we will resume in 15 minutes. 15 minutes. Ms. Korner, would you prefer to discuss the motion soon after we finish with this witness or towards the end of the sitting? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it matters much. It depends how long, Your Honours, and Mr. Ackerman think the discussion will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does matter because if the discussion takes a long time, it means that we might have to -- a witness here waiting and with no guarantee that he would be heard. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already been brought to the court. He's not actually in the waiting room yet but he's at the court, I believe. Your Honours, I simply -- if the -- Mr. Ackerman, I don't know how much longer with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour it looks like I may have 45 minutes -- 30 to 45 minutes left and with regard to the issue that we need to discuss in open court, we -- it seems to me we've covered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it should take us much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't anticipate any way and it's not my intention to allow either of you to take much time in discussing it. I want to make sure that we don't keep the gentleman who will be testifying after Mr. Odobasic here and then find ourselves in the situation where we have to tell him you've come here for nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 6.00 then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman has got another 35 minutes to which I'd add on another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forty-five he said probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then it perhaps -- I'd rather not keep the witness hanging around the Court unless we will then maybe lose sometime but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if we start at 5 past 4.00, then I reckon we have until quarter to 5.00 before we finish with Mr. Odobasic. I suppose we can thrash the motion, what needs to be said about it, not more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In no more than 20 minutes. Which would bring us to five past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I think the been could probably start, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if we break for a quarter of an hour then, he can start at 5.25 and we finish at 6.30. He will testify for an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's at least worth getting him settled in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that okay with you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. We will break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I just mention this? Unfortunately what I wasn't aware of, VWS brought the next witness here somewhat earlier and he was put into the waiting room. Your Honour, Mr. Nicholls has spoken to him and his preference to be it start tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he prefers to start in the morning and you can find us a courtroom, he would start in the morning, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If, Your Honours, are -- if that's acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is definitely acceptable to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I suppose, hasn't got any problems with that. So Ms. Korner you can communicate to Mr. Nicholls our decision. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go to your Sarajevo statement, which -- do you still have it or is it gone now? Okay. I want to talk to you some more about dismissals. It's page 4 of the English statement. I think a little later in your version. It begins with the language, "Head doctor, Velibor Milic." Can you find that "Head doctor, Velibor Milic?" Let me know.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said was, "Head doctor, Velibor Milic, one of the most prominent citizens of Serbian nationality was removed from his position as director of the Prnjavor health centre" and then it goes on to give the reason why. True?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... removed from his position; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say he was dismissed. It says here that he was removed from his position of director.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the word I used both times. Maybe it was translated incorrectly to you. I read the word removed just like it says there. Let's move forward, please. We talked a little earlier about the Sloga footwear factory. If you go over to characteristics of the Prnjavor economy, you'll see that again. Previously employed 1.370 workers, now 200. So 1.170 people were no longer employed there; right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they lost their jobs fully or whether they were simply put on waiting lists. You have to check that with the legal department in Sloga.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, all we have to rely on, sir, is the language of your statement in which you said it employed 1.370 and now employs 200. Certainly, it's the case that out of 1.370 people, only 200 were working at the Sloga footwear factory as of September of 1994, when you made this statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I will repeat: There could have been 200 in the plant itself, whereas the rest would have maintained their status of employees, they could have still been employed but not working. They could have been put on waiting lists whereas there was certainly a number of them who had been dismissed. The term here used was "employs only 200." That means 200 is involved in the manufacturing process. So we have to specify what number of people was dismissed and what number of people was put on waiting lists, meaning they were temporarily laid off for about a month or so while they were still in the status of an employed person, even maintaining their benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes, and I guess we can accept that. The fact is that that Sloga footwear factory was dependent upon sales to acquire the funds to pay its employees, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Sloga was a footwear factory and the salaries were dependent on the footwear produced and sold. That's how it was while I was still employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, while you were employed there, there were about 1370 people working there. What percentage of those people would you say were of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were definitely a convincing majority. I can't tell you the exact percentage but perhaps we could look at the ethnic composition in the town of Prnjavor at the time and presume that that composition was reflected in the ethnic composition of employees at Sloga. We never made such ethnic analysis of the composition, the one that you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the case that people instead of being completely dismissed were, what did you say, furloughed or something like that, if they were not completely dismissed but had no work, what would they do?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on their ethnic background. The majority of workers who were Serbs were given a wartime assignment. They went to military units and were probably paid something for that. I know that in the past, when people were called to attend military training and exercises, we used to get a compensation from that from the Secretariat of National Defence. I don't know if this procedure was maintained during wartime. I assume that it was. And I don't know what the status was of those who were temporarily laid off or furloughed, I don't know whether they were paid while they had their status but this is something that could be easily verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So with Sloga we've got 1170 people who are no longer going to work, whatever their status might be. With the Standard furniture factory, it completely halted production so we have 200 people that are no longer going to work; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wife of my brother didn't go to work because she was given a decision on terminating her status. After that, they discontinued the production process. I don't know whether the people continued going to the plant facility itself. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, we could get through there a lot faster if you and I would get on the same page. I am talking only about the number of people who were employed in these enterprises before the war and the number who were employed there apparently around September of 1994, when you gave this statement. What you said was that there were 200 workers there before the war, and now production halted completely. The only question I'm asking you, that's 200 people who are no longer working; right? At least at Standard.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that the production in the Standard factory was discontinued. Now, whether they did something else instead of that, I don't know. The figures I have given you are based on my assessments, whereas the precise figures can be obtained in enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Pionir ready made clothes factory had employed 300 and you said it was now closed so that's another 300 people who are no longer going to work, the majority of whom are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the director of Pionir, Novak Bozic was removed and Novak Bozic is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Metalka chain factory used to employ 260, then it employed 130, so 130 people were no longer going to work.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't formulate this properly. Let's see what it says here. No, no. I'm sorry, you're correct. 130 is the right number. You're right. I think that the total figure -- I thought that the total figure was 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Jelsingrad crane factory employed 180 before the war and is not working now so 180 people are not going to work?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the director Milorad Savkovic was dismissed, who is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was promoted, in fact. He went to a better job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at your statement, it says, its director Milorad Savkovic, about 40 years old, born in the village of Rizevci, Prnjavor municipality, was dismissed. And then it does say he was appointed to replace Milan Plancic at another place. You're correct. The Gradip GIK building construction industrial combine used to employ 350, not working now, another 350 workers not going to work?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the Promet trading company, its director, Mladjan, I think it's Debeljak, a Serb, was dismissed?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go to page 8, it's the English version page 8, it's that page where we were talking about the 300 Chetniks killed in clashes with soldiers of the BH Army, that might help you find it, it's on page 11,?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 8 or page 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of your version.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right under that sentence about the 300 Chetniks, you said this to the investigators: "In late September and early October of 1992, work obligations were introduced in Prnjavor. All the Muslim men laid off by the various firms were formed into work platoons as well as all other Muslims aged 15 to 60 who were fit for work." Correct? I'm only asking you if that's true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
