utterances.text: Okay. I want to go back to page 28 of your testimony yesterday, on the LiveNote, but the last thing you said about people who were departing Prnjavor was that they could only go via Serbia and Hungary to the western countries. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They could also go to central Bosnia, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first exchange involving central Bosnia was the one in which I was exchanged on the 27th of July, 1994. Prior to that, nobody else went to the liberated territory in central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that because they couldn't go there or because they did not want to go there because they knew they would be conscripted into the Bosnian army and they didn't want to fight?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my assessment was that 150 to 200.000 people were exchanged in that location where I was exchanged, going to central Bosnia. The rest went to western Europe because there was no other option except going there, through Hungary and Serbia. As soon as it was possible to leave, and most of the people went through Travnik, people came to Zenica en masse, and I personally took over them, hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was this: Was that because they couldn't go there or because they did not want to go there because they knew they would be conscripted into the Bosnian army and they didn't want to fight? Can you just kind of give me a simple answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't permitted to go to the free territory because they would probably take part and fight for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. This corridor to Serbia, how was that corridor cut off in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How was it cut off? I can give you my opinion, sir, but I'm no military expert. I'm not a strategist. If you wish my opinion, I will gladly give it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Give it to me.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known that the corridor went from Belgrade to the SAO Krajina and the Serbs did everything they could to ensure that it would pass through the territory that had a majority Serb population, and if we look at the territory going through Prnjavor municipality, from Banja Luka to Prnjavor and Doboj, as I've said yesterday, that road went through the territory that had majority of Serb population except for four villages. The problem arose when that road came between Doboj and Modrica because it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had to go through three municipalities which are predominantly populated by Croats. Part of Derventa municipality, Modrica, Odzak, Samac. Since in 1992, a conflict broke out in that territory, that was probably the reason for cutting off the corridor, starting in 1992 until after the war, I never visited the area of Derventa, Modrica, Odzak, municipalities as well as Orasje, so I don't know what the situation was like where and who cut off the corridor and where or why. However, I know that Serbs did not have a majority in those municipalities, and that was probably the reason why that corridor was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you speak of the SAO Krajina, you're speaking of a part of Croatia, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I mean the Knin Krajina and then the road goes through Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, with regard to this corridor, in your 30 January, 1999 statement, on page 6, you talked about that, and here is what you said in your statement. "In May, we couldn't communicate with any other Bosniak municipality. All communications were cut off. I can't remember the exact date but this area was cut off physically because the corridor didn't yet exist." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find it, please. Let me find the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help you a little bit. I probably can't. There is a really short paragraph talking about Goran Nikolic, who was beaten at a polling station. It's just below that beginning with, "In May we couldn't communicate with any other Bosniak municipality."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's page 5, Goran Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next paragraph, I think you got there. It would be the next paragraph, "In May we couldn't communicate with any other Bosniak municipality." You see that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think the witness still has his AID -- his Sarajevo statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you're looking at the wrong statement. You're looking at the Sarajevo statement instead of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking about the one given on the 30th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He has it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In English it's page 6 so it should be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it says that the area was cut off physically because the corridor didn't yet exist. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because that corridor didn't exist, it wasn't just communications that were cut off. There was a -- began to be a lack of all kinds of essential supplies, didn't there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably wasn't possible to get the supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk to you now about the Wolves of Vucjak. In the statement you have in front of you, and if you want to find it, I'll help you, but I think you probably don't need to, in that statement, speaking of the Wolves of Vucjak you commented that Veljko Milankovic was well known in the area even before the war as a criminal. That's true, right? It's on page 3, if you want to find it, page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. It was just the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And tell me what you mean by him being well known in the area as a criminal. Had he been convicted of crimes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had he been convicted? I can't claim with certainty but I believe that he was, for many perpetrated crimes. Yesterday I clarified. My city inspectorate filed two criminal reports against that gentleman due to unlawful cutting of timber. I didn't verify this information here but I heard that there were at least 30 various charges filed against the gentleman. I learned from a policeman before the war that this policeman filed criminal complaint against him for a rape attempt perpetrated by Veljko Milankovic. He also broke law and order, participated in bar brawls, that was quite a frequent occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So his reputation around town was as a criminal character, dangerous, would engage in violence, things of that nature? He had that reputation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this criminal character created a paramilitary organisation called the wolves and I assume that he recruited other people of like character and like mind to join him in that organisation. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, he didn't establish that organisation. I said it quite clearly on the first day of my testimony. The leaders of the SDS established that paramilitary formation. They simply used Veljko Milankovic was a weapon in their hands. They gave him arms to establish that paramilitary formation, and you saw a document to that effect yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this group began once they were formed harassing the local population, including Serbs at times; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me think for a minute. I know that the Serbs had been harassed by the other paramilitary formation. Yes, I remember that there was talk that they had harassed Serbs who failed to respond to mobilisation. However, I cannot corroborate this. I have no specific proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the case, is it not, that by this time, with this group operating in Prnjavor, that law and order in Prnjavor had basically broken down and was non-existent?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were frequent incidents. We can't say that we managed to maintain the same law and order we had before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The police made an effort, didn't they? They arrested several of these paramilitaries of Milankovic's and even arrested him at one point, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specified the time when that took place. The police did try and managed to arrest these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then what they did in response to that was attack the police station, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they attacked the police station, and then perhaps a day later, after the attack, Milankovic and some of his men were arrested. The police in a way managed to establish relations that were a bit normal after that conflict. However, it didn't last long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Mr. Brdjanin made serious efforts to have Mr. Milankovic arrested, to stop his activities?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard Mr. Brdjanin. I knew Mr. Brdjanin only from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear in the media about Mr. Brdjanin's speech at the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on 15 November, 1991, when he started firing at Grahovac by asking him what it was that he was doing establishing some paramilitary unit, spending money on it, buying uniforms and other things with Sendic and Mladjenovic, without anyone's orders sending them across the Sava and what they did there? Do you remember him making that speech and hearing about that speech in the media?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard nor saw, nor could I hear or see any such thing. From the -- after the address of Mr. Brdjanin in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I stopped following all the sessions of these political organs because it really irritated me, and as a normal person, I didn't wish to listen to such political speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you said that in -- a little later, this group called the White Eagles, another paramilitary group, came to town and started causing troubles, and they were also attacking people, including on occasion some Serbs, and that this Milankovic Wolves group basically arrested them and threw them out of town; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the first incursion when we were mistreated and the second one when they arrested them and took them in the direction of Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally, in January or February of 1993, Veljko Milankovic was wounded in battle and died in a hospital in Belgrade, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that it was at the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were just a bunch of hoodlums, weren't they, this Wolves of Vucjak group?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if you know what I mean by hoodlums, a bunch of criminals running around committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the -- those were people who were acting within the system, a group of criminals who were part of the military system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, they weren't always part of the military system. They became part of the 1st Krajina Corps at some point, though, didn't they? Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I think that it was at that time in the fighting for Derventa, when battles were fought for piercing the corridor. It was then that they committed crimes. As part of my regular duties, I exhumed seven such victims in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, at the time signature is 17.57.10 in the LiveNote, you were asked this question: "Before we will talk about the events which occurred after the elections, I would like to ask you whether there were any paramilitary formations in Prnjavor before the elections." Your answer was this: Before the elections I used to see some people bearing arms which under normal circumstances was banned. Most often I would see them in the villages of Kremna and in that area, something, it's not readable. However they claimed that those people were the so-called reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army which wasn't the case. You remember telling the judges that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before the election that is would have been a time when the government was still under the authority of the League of Communists; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More precisely, in 1989, at the time the famous rally was held at Gazimestan, there were very frequent military exercises going on at the time. People were being armed. There were, however, a lot of honourable people who did not abuse this arming, but there were also others who often opened fire. It was at the time when the so-called communist government was in power, and in that period, the police tried as best as they could, to ensure that everyday life was still normal. I don't remember any murders or attacks at that time but there were -- there was a lot of intimidation by way of shooting and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that that government would not have put up with anything like the open carrying of arms that you described?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're forgetting, sir, that at the time there were a lot of people in this government who followed the platform of Mr. Milosevic, and who were trying, doing their best to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer it.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you a clear answer. There was a split

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes or no. Isn't it the case that the government would not have put up with anything like the open carrying of arms that you described? You can either say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is telling you that he can't give you a straight answer of yes or no, Mr. Ackerman, so please go ahead and give him the answer that you think is precise, according to your knowledge of the events. He's telling you straight and plain that there was no uniformity in the government. There were different currents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a no answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I accept a no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is an answer. So please go ahead and answer his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've finished with my question. He said no.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me just one more sentence to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, in respect of the persons who at the time wore uniforms, it was very difficult for the regular police to intervene because it was the military police that was in charge of such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said the Wolves were involved in fighting in September of 1992. What battles were going on in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot tell you where they were involved exactly but the fighting went on not only in September but until the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and they participated in the large -- in a large number of theatres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess when they were away fighting in these large number of theatres, they were not bothering the citizens of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on whether all of them were deployed in the battlefield or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke about them engaged in looting. You don't contend, do you, that they were looting under orders from General Talic and the 1st Krajina Corps, do you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 3 of your September 1994 statement, that's the one in Sarajevo, you speak of a Ljuban Milosevic. You say, "Ljuban Milosevic, the SDS spokesman also worked for radio. Very often visited and sent reports from the battlefield." What battlefield was it you're referring to when you talk about him reporting from the battlefield? Would that have been in the corridor or over in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reported from the battlefields in Croatia even before that, when these formations from Prnjavor participated in the war over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go down just a little ways, sir, you begin a paragraph with this language, "After the assumption of political power, personnel changes in the SUP" and you go on and have a discussion there. What you're referring to as "the assumption of political power" was a result of a democratic election where the SDS won the most of the seats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the result of a democratic election but the result of the behaviour of the people who had been elected at this election. The election itself was -- had been a democratic election but I was speaking of the results of the behaviour of certain people after that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But they didn't assume political power. They were elected there by the voters of Prnjavor in a fair election, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about political functions here but you asked me about police functions. These are not political functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say at that time that the SJB commander was a person named Boro Tramosljanin; right? A Serb. Same paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you may have misspoken. Not the commander but a commanding officer. That was the name of the office within the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to look at that paragraph. It's the same one that begins with "after the assumption of political power," and you will see a sentence beginning with, "At that time, the SJB commander was Boro Tramosljanin son of Milan."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was a --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commanding officer, komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they made efforts to replace him, didn't they? They didn't want him in that position, the people who had taken power.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But they didn't have the ability to dismiss him without the approval of the Minister of the Interior in Sarajevo, Alija Delimustafic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Alija Delimustafic is a Bosniak and was at the time a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It took five months before they could get the approval of Alija Delimustafic to dismiss Boro Tramosljanin and replace him with Nenad Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you'll go over the next page, you talk about the creation of what you refer to as the Serbian MUP, and you say that all members of Muslim nationality were given the opportunity to sign the oath of loyalty which they refused to do and after which their employment was terminated. Are you saying there that not even one non-Serb signed that oath of loyalty and remained with the police?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot say that, but I don't know whether there were any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you do know is that some people who were Serbs disagreed with what was happening, and they were also dismissed, and you even named them, Miroslav Petrovic, Dragan Vrhovac, Rodoljub Jugovic, Zika Milijasevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the issue regarding whether or not one would be dismissed from the police was not their ethnicity but whether or not they were willing to express their loyalty to the new government?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that there were Muslims who were part of the Army of Republika Srpska, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony, you were asked about whether -- and this is at page 16, line 17, line 14, you were asked about whether during this period of time, 1991 or 1992, civilians of Serb ethnicity would be armed, and in part, your answer was this, starting at line 20: "My best friend, a Serb, he fled Prnjavor when they tried to give him a machine-gun by force." I'm curious, how do you try to give one a machine-gun by force? How do you force one to take a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you will have to find out how that was possible. As I indicated, during that period of time weapons were being distributed before the hunting lodge in Prnjavor from a trailer truck so those who wanted to get weapons. This friend of mine, a professor, is a pacifist and he simply didn't want to go to war against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my question is --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He confirmed this. He's now living in Belgrade, and at the time when the war was going on in Kosovo, he didn't want to go there. He managed to avoid being sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question, sir, is not that I was asked to take a machine-gun but your language that they tried to give him one by force and I'm curious as to how you force someone to take a gun. Do you threaten to shoot them if they don't take this gun with bullets? How do you make them take a gun that they don't want? How do you force them to do that? And what kind after fool would do that in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask him whether they threatened that they would shoot but apparently he was told that they needed a couple of intellectuals within their military units and that he had to take this machine-gun and to join his battle for a sacred cause. He was a well-known person in this village. He had been a teacher to a number of generations there, and it was necessary to have this weapon placed in his hands in order to convince those who were still hesitant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what this really was was -- he was being mobilised and he was refusing to be mobilised and fled the territory to avoid that? That's what really happened, huh?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mobilisation is carried out pursuant to a specific procedure, pursuant to call-up papers. The gentleman happened to be there with his wife and children, wearing civilian clothes, on his way to the village of Sarici and he came across three vehicles, horse drawn carts actually, from which weapons were being distributed. It's not a regular way to mobilise people. I would rather call it an anarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you move to something else, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm doing that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 17, line 21 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked if you ever heard of any reasons why the Serbs armed themselves, and your answer was, "Yes, Serbs claimed that attack on Prijedor --" and that would be Prnjavor, I'm sure -- Your Honour, it's getting to the point where even I'm starting to say Prijedor when it should be Prnjavor it's getting difficult, but the transcript does say Prijedor and I think it should be Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, again it should be Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Serbs claimed that an attack on Prnjavor from a direction of Derventa is imminent. They were saying they were arming themselves in order to defend themselves from the Ustashas, referring to the population of Derventa." Now, one thing that was going on in this battle for the corridor was that there was very heavy fighting at and around Derventa, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had armed themselves long time before the battle for corridor took place. In a neighbouring village, in Derventa, at the border line with the Prnjavor municipality, Dragan Djuric, a deputy lived, and he made sure that people were armed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that answer?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with respect to Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, I appreciate that, now let me have you answer the question I asked you. One thing that was going on in this battle for the corridor was that there was very fighting at and around Derventa, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the corridor was pierced, there had been fighting in and around Derventa, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Derventa was a community that was majority Croat, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was but I'm not sure. Compared to Serbs -- maybe it was. Yes, you should check the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was located around 30 kilometres from Prnjavor, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 33 kilometres, at least that's what the sign said on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was actually captured by Croatian forces and the corridor was closed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they were Croatian forces or some other forces. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that it was captured from the Serbs, from the Serb forces, you certainly know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was initially held by Serbs. I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear the sounds of the battles from Derventa in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, the so-called lunas, at least that's what the military experts called them, would fly over the town of Prnjavor, having been fired from the village Strbac. We could see the traces, and they must have ended up somewhere above Slavonski Brod. People who were later sent to Derventa, to plunder abandoned apartments told us this, who were sent there as a work obligation to plunder on behalf of the authorities, and I often saw them flying over our town, having been fired from Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I had asked you if you had ever seen things flying over your town regarding these battles, that would have been the appropriate answer. Now let me ask you the question I -- again that I wanted the answer to. Did you hear the sounds of battles from Derventa?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware in Prnjavor --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, nothing else. This is all I ever heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I asked you. What you heard. Were you aware of any visits to Prnjavor at any time between 1992 and the time you left by the international committee of the Red Cross, the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I'd been beaten up, they came to me and they conducted an interview in Prnjavor. Whether they came before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And about when would that? You were beaten up more than once. About when was it that they interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the fourth beating, the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn from that what it was the ICRC was trying to accomplish in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They talked to me in order to relocate me and my brother because we were in the worst condition, to take us outside Prnjavor and they asked me whether I wanted to be moved. I think that they mentioned Zagreb, and when I wanted -- when I told them that I wanted my entire family to be relocated, they said, "Sir, we will do our best, we will try to arrange this with Serb authorities." But after that, they never visited me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The last thing I want to talk to you about and I think we can do this rather briefly, is this: At page 33 of your testimony yesterday, you were asked about the events that happened in Lisnja. You said that were you not there when Lisnja was attacked by but a few days later you passed through the village and you saw that 54 houses had been burned down. Did you actually count the houses to get to that number, 54?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the -- one of the victims in Lisnja, whose house is close to torched houses was a certain Halilovic. I was a close friend of his for a number of years and I went to look for him and since after I found him we started analysing how many houses had been burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, please. It is a very simple question: You have been asked whether you counted -- you counted the houses or you didn't. Did you count them, physically count the houses? Or were you told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't count. We made a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Whatever that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you made a list that included 54 houses?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was the last time you'd been to Lisnja before this visit?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was there at the rally representing the SDP. I was the guest invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was when?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the first multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Madam Richterova, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, thank you. I do not have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. I do not really have any particular questions except that before you leave this courtroom, I request a clarification from you, and that's regarding the photos that you produced yesterday. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday, I asked you a very simple question, namely whether you had shown any of those photos to any of the investigators of the Prosecution, either prior, previous to your coming here to The Hague to give evidence, or since your arrival here in The Hague, and your answer to me was -- your reply was in a sense that you recall having given those photos to the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina on some previous occasion but that you didn't recall having handed those photos to the Office of the Prosecutor at any time. Then it was pointed out to you by Mr. Ackerman that this did not correspond with what was included in one of the statements that you had released to the Office of the Prosecutor. And a part from that statement was even read out to you. And it is my feeling that you did not come up with a proper explanation. I'm giving you the opportunity once more to go back to the same question that I asked you yesterday. Do you confirm that your statement of yesterday, that you never gave any of those photos to any of the officers of the Prosecution or any of the investigators of the Prosecution, or do you want to correct your statement or make some other kind of declaration?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Sarajevo in 1994, I brought a large number of photographs with me, various photographs, including these ones, and I turned over the negatives to our investigative organs, they gave me one copy which is the first copy I showed to you yesterday. They asked me several times whether I would permit them to turn over these photographs Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to The Hague Tribunal and other investigative organs and I agreed to that. Yesterday, I thought for quite a long time, and I could not remember. It is possible that at the time when I gave the statement, those photographs were turned over to The Hague investigators. Every interview we had with The Hague Tribunal was organised by investigators. They would come in if requested so by the investigators, and so on. I was told that some 16 photographs could be turned over, and I signed a written consent to that. What I'm claiming with full certainty is that the only copy is the one I have here on me, and out of those photographs, I did not surrender any to anybody else except for you yesterday. This statement is quite long, and it is now difficult for me to remember every detail contained in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you recall having been shown these photos after you arrived here in The Hague and before you started giving evidence? Were you ever shown these photos?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to my arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, after your arrival here in the Hague.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took them out and I attempted to show them to the OTP, the copies I showed to you yesterday. However, I was told that there was no need to show them because they were not related to 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman, since I brought up this matter again, I give you the opportunity to put one or two further questions to the witness related only to this matter of the photos and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. Further cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you'll recall yesterday that I quoted from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The statement of 15th March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your statement of 15 March, 1999 to the Prosecutor and I have in front of me a -- I don't know. Do you have that? Do you have the 15 March, 1999 statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you also to have the English version of it, please. Now, the very last--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- sentence is what I'm interested in but I'd like you to look at the English version of that statement and tell us if that is your signature that appears directly under that last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the English version, it says this: "As well, I am providing copies of 17 photographs which I and my brother took of injuries, myself, my brother, my father, and my brother's wife received as a result of beatings by Serb police and authorities in Prnjavor." Now, that's what this indicates you told the investigators of the Tribunal and what you did, that you surrendered 17 photographs to them. Now, my question is this: In view of that, at page 63, line 5 of your testimony yesterday, with regard to that statement, you said that that statement referred to the photos that were shown here in court yesterday but I personally didn't hand them over at that time. Now, that's what you told us yesterday, and how on earth can you reconcile those two things? By saying at one time on a document you signed you did turn them over and then by telling these judges yesterday that you didn't.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just clarified, all of these documents were turned by me in 1994 to our investigative organs, and in 1999, they were brought here, and this is the first time that I see that these other documents are mentioned here as well. Now I just can't remember whether photographs were among those documents turned over. I didn't really go over that to see what our investigative organs turned over to the investigators of The Hague at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If I understand what you're saying, you're saying that it wasn't you that turned them over but they may have been turned over by your investigators who came with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I don't understand your explanation at all. Are you contending that you turned them over or you didn't turn them over? Which of those are you contending is the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He told you he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Or you just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it there, Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Odobasic, that brings us to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Tribunal, on my own behalf and on behalf of the two judges sitting with me in this trial, Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and Judge Taya from Japan, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence in our endeavours in search of the truth. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour. I'm told that the only way to get this clarified is to deal with this now. At the end of his testimony before you started asking him about these photographs, he had said he'd gone to a rally in Lisnja, and the transcript says that he went there representing SDP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- that's what I heard, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told that he said he went there representing SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, what the witness said: He went to the SDA rally representing SDP, the only thing that didn't make it into the transcript is SDA rally and it's on page 62, line 16. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Odobasic? Was the rally an SDA rally that you attended in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally, I said yesterday that we were invited to attend as guests, and there were five of us guests at the SDA rally, representing the SDP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me take up from where I left. On behalf of this Trial Chamber, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence. You will be escorted out of this courtroom by the usher and you will receive all the attention that you require in order to enable you to return to your country of residence. Once more, I thank you, and I wish you -- we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all for this experience, which is a new one for me as a lawyer. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now, yes, I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we could have just a very brief recess and so I could have some additional consultation with my client? I hadn't quite finished before we came back from the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say a brief recess, how long do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fifteen, 20 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I suggest it's 15 rather than 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fifteen should be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fifteen, perfect. We will resume in 15 minutes from now. It's now 5.32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll remain in open session until and unless there is a request to go into private session for a part or the whole of the rest of the debate on this motion for adjournment of trial. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since this is the first time the matter has been dealt with in any detail in open court, and on the record, I just want to give just a very brief background. On 24 February, 2003, which I think was Tuesday of that week, by memorandum I advised Your Honours and the Prosecutor that I have a serious medical condition that is going to require that I return to Texas and undergo some surgery which will require a seven- or eight-day hospital stay following the surgery and then a fairly significant recuperation period thereafter which is set out in great detail in the memo Your Honours have I won't go into any more detail because you know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that letter I also set out for Your Honours a plan which I believe would work for the continuation of this case and some of that plan has been accepted and implemented already, and that is my bringing another member on to the Defence team in this case, who hopefully in the future will be able to provide significant assistance to me and to the Trial Chamber with regard to continuing this case. Basically, then, we had multiple meetings, I think two, in chambers and then one formal Rule 65 ter conference yesterday where this matter was discussed further, and at greater length. In the meantime, I have had a number of meetings with Mr. Brdjanin regarding his wishes regarding what would happen as a result of this situation, which none of us wanted, of course, but it came upon us and now it has to be faced. Mr. Brdjanin expressed his wishes regarding this matter. I then filed yesterday a motion for adjournment of the trial. It was filed confidentially, Your Honours, because attached to is a memorandum which contains some information which I consider rather personal and would like to have kept within our small community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And it will remain within our small community, Mr. Ackerman, because it's not food for public consumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After hearing Mr. Brdjanin's wishes, I drafted a statement setting out those wishes in language which I believed contained what it was he wished to say to the Trial Chamber as concisely as I possibly could. What he said to you and says to you is this: "John Ackerman was and is my choice to serve as lead counsel in my case. I understand that under the Rules of this Tribunal, accused have the right to choose their counsel and Mr. Ackerman is my choice. I object to any proceedings going forward in this case unless my chosen counsel is present in The Hague or unless his presence is specifically waived by me. I understand Mr. Ackerman's medical condition and I object to going forward with this case after the sitting on 14 March, 2003, until Mr. Ackerman is able to return to The Hague and assist with my defence either in or out of court." And that was signed by Mr. Brdjanin and then attached to the motion for adjournment, which I filed yesterday, Your Honours. Mr. Brdjanin understands and I understand that paragraph 2 of that document is an objection to any and all proceedings going forward in this case unless his lead counsel is present in The Hague, and that would include the cross-examination of witnesses, hearings on motions, or any other matters that would be dealt with ordinarily in court. And then finally, and I want this to be brief, Your Honour, there is no sense going at great length on this because we have all looked at this in many different ways, the request that I make, and that Mr. Brdjanin makes in conjunction with me, is contained in the wherefore clause of the motion that I filed yesterday, and that is: "That the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin, by and through his lead counsel, John Ackerman hereby respectfully requests that this case be adjourned following the sitting on 14 March, 2003, until a time that his lead counsel is able to return to The Hague and assist with his case as is outlined in the memorandum which was attached as Exhibit A," and that's the memorandum I spoke of that was shared with the judges, and I should only, I suppose, add that that memorandum projects that the case can resume in about one month, which means that we could resume around the 15th of April, and that looks at first glance like a one month delay, but immediately following the 15th of April we have scheduled a one week delay which I have suggested should be abandoned so actually the delay would only be a three week hiatus in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner? Would you like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, of course, as Mr. Ackerman has pointed out, we dealt with this at considerable length yesterday in a Rule 65 ter conference which of course is a matter of record in the future. For the purpose of this hearing, first of all on behalf of the Prosecution we wish to express our sincere regrets that Mr. Ackerman is in this position and we trust that medical treatment that he requires will be successful and completed. That leads me on to the second point. It's not for the defendant, the accused, to object and to have his objection automatically upheld. It's a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide whether there would be an injustice in continuing with co-counsel, and I emphasise those words, co-counsel, carrying on in Mr. Ackerman's absence. The situation is complicated because of the number of occasions on which Your Honours have raised with the Defence whether or not if there were to be an absence of Mr. Ackerman, his co-counsel would be unable to take over because of what happened on earlier occasions when there was a different co-counsel, and the assurance was really effectively from the 18th of April onwards, that that would be the case. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution does not object to this adjournment if there is an amplification of Mr. Brdjanin's reason for objecting to the continuation of this case in Mr. Ackerman's absence. It's not enough in our submission simply to say I do not want it to proceed in the absence of lead counsel. There must be a reason. And putting it as neutrally as I can, Your Honour, if that reason is because, however experienced co-counsel may be in his own jurisdiction, he is inexperienced in these type of proceedings, and because of his lack of ability to speak English, he is unable to deal with any motions or any documents that are in English, well, then, Your Honour, that is in our submission a good reason. But that has to be stated, in our submission, clearly and squarely by Mr. Brdjanin, because there are consequences that follow from that, which I think it's only right that the Court should have fairly and squarely in front of it at this stage, and I'm going to put them very shortly but Your Honour I think that is the first thing. It's our submission, it's not enough simply to say I object to going ahead. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There has to be a reason. So I don't know whether Your Honours want to hear it from Mr. Ackerman or from Mr. Brdjanin direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop there for the time being. Mr. Ackerman, I address you of course and not your client directly. Are you in a position to tell us whether your client would like to respond to what has been pointed out by Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To answer your question directly, Your Honour, my client would make a statement to the Court if you think that would be helpful to you. He's prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you been following, Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that you are prepared or you would like to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am prepared to make a statement and I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So let's proceed with your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me express my gratitude to you and Ms. Korner for having enabled me -- well, it's all the same to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my opinion, Your Honour, that if it had been anyone else here, as Defence counsel, and I want to be perfectly clear, if it were the best possible Defence lawyer on the world, I would request for an adjournment until the return of Mr. Ackerman, and if you will allow me, please, two or three sentences to explain this, I am aware of the fact that I am the one who chooses the lead counsel and I have done that. We have been together for 14 months, Mr. Ackerman and myself. I did have a lawyer who was suspended, and then another one arrived and I think that he has been carrying out his duty also with respect to the laws in the former Yugoslavia and I have no problem with that. I have nothing against Mr. Ackerman designating a different lawyer when he comes back for continuing interviewing and examining witnesses, but I would be the happiest if the team sitting at this table should remain complete. I did not want to express any doubts in respect of anyone but I think that it is a very important moment in the trial. This is the end of the Prosecution case, and I think it's very important for the lead counsel to remain on the team. For my personal safety and also because of the trust that I have and the authority that they have, and because of the procedure of submitting requests and applications and because of how we have been proceeding so far. I am not doubting anyone's qualities but I think you too can have a very realistic assessment of the situation. If this was the beginning of the case, I think that the situation would be different, but I am the person who is in a hurry here. I would wish -- would like the proceedings to be expeditious as possible. I don't know whether I can influence your decision but I would like to express my wish for that adjournment until Mr. Ackerman returns and I would also like this team to remain in its current composition because any further changes would really cause anxiety in myself. I think I would be afraid of any new changes. The material is considerable and I have been studying this material for the past four years. Therefore, I have agreed with Mr. Ackerman, I am not going to meddle in his affairs when he comes back, and I don't think that it would be forbidden to anyone else, any other lawyer, to examine witnesses, but that will be the decision of Mr. Ackerman. I am a lay person, as far as law is concerned. I'm a civil engineer. I am aware also of the costs involved and I'm aware of the fact that this trial has been going on for quite sometime, but at any rate, I should like to appeal to you once again to grant my request and then -- and that we proceed as suggested by Mr. Ackerman. If there is anything else you want to help me with, I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I ask through Your Honour to perhaps put a question to Mr. Brdjanin in the light of what he said? If we were to undertake that we were -- would only call -- he's right, in a sense we are heading towards major witnesses but if we were to undertake that during the absence of Mr. Ackerman, we would call only crime-base witnesses, none of whom directly implicated him, would he be content for Mr. Trbojevic to cross-examine or is he, and it's not quite clear, leaving the decision to Mr. Ackerman to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully request that you not ask that question. First of all, I want to say two or three things. What Mr. Brdjanin says about he and I being together for 40 months has to me just huge weight. That 40 months has been 40 months in which I have learned an enormous amount about this case. I have an enormous data base about this case inside my head so that when someone who is new to this team has a question about how to proceed with regard to any particular matter, I can answer that question only because I have this 40 months experience with this team. You know that in the course of what's about to happen to me, there will be at least a period of two weeks when I will not be in any kind of a condition to advise anyone in this case in any respect whatsoever. So that if the case is going forward, it's going forward with someone who has absolutely no grounding regarding all of the issues in this case. A co-counsel who joined this case in April, even if they could read English, with all the other responsibilities, couldn't have read all the transcripts and couldn't be as grounded in this case as I am. Second of all, the proposition that we should do a whole series of crime-base witnesses in my absence and then I would take over all these other witnesses when I came back, has an accordion effect which is devastating to the Defence. What Ms. Korner is suggesting that we take all of the extraordinarily difficult witnesses that require the most exhausting preparation and work and collapse them all to the end of the case so that when I come back, not yet fully recovered, it will be my job to cross-examine one after another after another of the most important witnesses in the case. Now, that's great advantage for the Prosecutor to be able to do that. It's a huge advantage. And a great disservice and injustice to Mr. Brdjanin. So I'd ask that you not ask him that question and that you simply grant the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I leave it in Your Honour's hands as to whether that question is put. In fact, there is sufficient crime-base evidence plus to take us even further than the four weeks. It's not that we would be going straight into expert evidence or anything like that. But, Your Honour, I do think it's important, I think it's important that it's made absolutely clear now what is going to happen in the future. As far as the month's adjournment is concerned, let me put it this way: I certainly wouldn't object if there is nobody who can take over for any reasons expressed by Mr. Brdjanin or by Mr. Ackerman but we have to look at the future. And at the moment, the future looks exceedingly bleak. This trial has now run for some just over a year, 15 months effectively. We had anticipated that we would finish the Prosecution case, I originally estimated Easter, that was wrong but certainly hopefully by the end of May so that would give time for the Rule 98 motions such as they may be. What is going to happen is plain as a pike staff in the light of the fact that Mr. Trbojevic, with the greatest of respect, is not the counsel that Mr. Ackerman needed before and needs now, for two reasons. And as I say this is meant with no disrespect to him, it's just a fact of life. He has not got the experience of practice before this Tribunal and he cannot read the language or speak the language, as a result of which of course any communication between Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Ackerman has to be done through an interpreter, apart from anything else. Your Honour, this is a document-heavy case. There are undoubtedly outstanding motions still to come. There are a number of expert witnesses to come. There are then the half-time submissions that have to be written and following that, if Your Honours decide that there is a case to answer on all or any of these charges, there will be the Defence case. It is quite impossible for Mr. Ackerman to do all of this with a co-counsel who cannot assist. The net effect is this: There will be undoubtedly, and Your Honour will have to grant them, applications, as there have been in the past, for further time so that Mr. Ackerman can deal with the paper work or the experts or whatever. That in itself will cause a further delay. There would, I anticipate, be applications of time for a man in the best of health, let alone a man who is perhaps not in the best of health. That has the effect of delaying this trial even further, keeping Mr. Brdjanin in the detention unit for a longer period of time, as an unconvicted man, and equally, as other Trial Chambers have pointed out, it delays the trials of other people who have been awaiting trial for even longer. Your Honours made it quite clear, and it has been done by other courts as well, that whoever was appointed co-counsel had to have the ability to at least stand in for a limited period of time, if lead counsel had to be absent, and it's quite apparent that this is not the case. So, Your Honour, I'm drawing Your Honours' attention to those matters and also the attention of the Registry and those responsible for the allocation of counsel because I think unless this matter is sorted out in the very, very near future, this case is going to go completely off the rails. I hear what Mr. Brdjanin says that he wants his team kept together. I sympathise with that. He's had two changes -- he's had a change already of counsel but it does seem to me that there must be an opportunity for Mr. Trbojevic to work, as it were, in the background and for someone to be in court possibly with the connections in Banja Luka, there are counsel who are available, who speak the language and who can really assist. So Your Honours, I make that point at this stage because I think it's important that somehow or other some clarification is reached of what is to happen. Your Honour, with the instant matter, Your Honour has heard what I have to say. Your Honours may or may not choose to ask Mr. Brdjanin the question but in the event that it is Mr. Brdjanin's wish that the trial not proceed with co-counsel only and Mr. Ackerman -- then we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, would you like to wind up? Do you think it is necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't think it's necessary. I think a lot of what Ms. Korner is telling you is really very, very speculative. I think I have set out a plan for you that allows this case to go forward and I think I even suggested to you that I believe we can conclude this case at the same time we would have had I not had this problem because I'm willing to make some commitments to you regarding time in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think speculation gets us no where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Our position is as follows: First, having heard both Ms. Korner and you, Mr. Ackerman, we don't think it is appropriate for us at this moment to address the question that Ms. Korner mentioned to Mr. Brdjanin. We do take into account, however, the substance of your objection to that question being put. Second thing we wanted to point out is the past events in this trial, where the circumstances were pretty much similar, referring first of all back to around about April of last year when the first -- the problem first arose as to what happens if the lead counsel is sick, is ill, for sometime. It was our belief at the time that both -- that all the instruments of -- relative instruments of this Tribunal, and in particular the directives and the policy of the Registrar, the office of the Registrar, pointed in no unclear terms that should the lead counsel be unable to attend to his duties, then even at short notice, the co-counsel ought to be in a position to take over. Not on a permanent basis because that would bring to nothing the whole role of the lead counsel. We had made this clear, and the point was reiterated and confirmed in due course by the office of the Registrar to us and to both of you, pointing out in particular that the appointment of any future co-counsel in this case had to be accompanied, and had to be predicated first to the assurance forthcoming from the lead counsel, who puts forward the name of a co-counsel, that that co-counsel would be in a position to take over even at short notice. I have the word of the Registrar that -- when I say the Registrar, it's his office which deals with these problems -- that before Mr. Trbojevic was appointed, he was given to understand that given time, Mr. Trbojevic would be in a position to take over. I've also gone through the transcripts, one in particular, which goes back to May of last year, where more or less Mr. Ackerman, you told us that Mr. Trbojevic was getting familiarised with the case. But obviously some problems because he didn't speak the English language and therefore he had problems with transcripts, but that in due course, all these problems would be solved and he would be in a position to take over. In fact, when earlier on this year, roughly a month ago, you needed to go to the States for some personal -- to have some personal matters related to your health attended to, following the assurance of the Prosecution that there would be a rescheduling of witnesses to be brought forward, it was agreed and it was suggested by yourself that Mr. Trbojevic would, for that particular week when you would be absent, take over the cross-examination. The situation seems to have changed since then, and we haven't been told why it has changed but it has obviously changed, because now the contention is that the accused has the right to interpret his right to have a counsel, whether it's of his own choosing or not or absolutely so is a matter which we don't need to go into, means also that he can force a situation where, if his lead counsel is absent, even for one day, then he can have the case stopped. Also, that if his lead counsel, as is in this case, would be absent for a whole month, then he also expects that his right to have a counsel of his own choosing translates also in a right to have the case stopped. We reiterate what we maintained earlier on in this case, that should there be a situation where the lead counsel is unable to attend to his duties, then it is the co-counsel who takes over, and it will be the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsibility of the Tribunal to see to it that there is no prejudice in proceeding in this manner to the accused. In this particular case, this is not being offered. What is being offered to this Tribunal is a situation whereby it has been decided by the Defence that, as a result of Mr. Ackerman's need to travel to the United States and be absent from attending to his duties for this month, there is no other solution but for this Trial Chamber to stop this case. This is not what we think should be the position, knowing that there is a co-counsel in this case that has, in the past, attended to duties of cross-examining witnesses. So our decision for the time being is to stop here, order that a copy of the transcript of today's debate, together with a copy of the transcript of the 65 ter meeting that we had yesterday, be communicated to the Registrar, who is expected to decide whether it is compatible for the role of the co-counsel to be directed not to indulge, to involve in -- not to exercise any cross-examining -- cross-examination of witnesses, and to report back to the Trial Chamber on this and on any action that the same office may deem appropriate. Following such report, the Trial Chamber will decide on the motion. That's our decision. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply make one comment? You said in what you just said that you know that Mr. Trbojevic cross-examined witnesses during an earlier week while I was gone, and that apparently the situation has changed and you've not been told why it has changed, and I thought I had done that and I want to make it clear why it has changed. It has changed because during that week I was in daily contact with my team here in The Hague. I was able to advise them on a daily basis. I was in instant e-mail contact, except for very brief times when I was undergoing testing, with the people here in The Hague. The difference this time is that there will be a two week period when I will not be able to be in contact. I thought I had made that clear. Apparently I had not. So I want it to make sure that that is clear both to you and for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is a very different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is different, indeed, Mr. Ackerman, but there is Ms. Baruch who you can instruct now and if problems are encountered then we find a solution but your client needs to understand that he cannot have the cake and eat it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Rules of this say that in a case of this nature, an accused is entitled to have two counsel. Now you're sighing he can go forward with one counsel. He can't go forward with one counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has three at the moment, Mr. Ackerman, not two. So that is our decision. The sitting stands adjourned, we will reconvene tomorrow, and Madam Registrar, please make sure that the transcripts are handed to the Registrar with the utmost urgency because this is a matter that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has been taken care of. Yesterday's transcript has been forwarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take your word for it. Thank you.
